sources.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
sources.text: OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion. Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg. In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target. TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds. The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago. OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point. The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market , with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future. sources.title: OpenAI reportedly raises $11B in new funding at $1.25T valuation
sources.text: OpenAI Group PBC has reportedly raised $11 billion as part of a funding round that could nearly double in size over the coming weeks, as s ources told Bloomberg that investors wired the funds to the company today. The tipsters didn’t name the backers. The list of possible participants includes Microsoft Corp., which contributed to at least four of OpenAI’s previous rounds. That included its most recent $122 billion raise in March, which also drew the participation of Nvidia Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and about two dozen others. It’s believed that OpenAI could raise up to $9 billion in additional funding as part of the round. The deal is expected to value the company at $1.25 billion. That potentially puts it on track to surpass Anthropic PBC’s market capitalization. Anthropic hopes to achieve a valuation of $1.5 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. However, several of its investors reportedly don’t consider that to be a realistic goal. According to the Wall Street Journal , one shareholder reportedly suggested that the company pursue a valuation closer to $1 trillion. Anthropic’s IPO filing revealed that its quarterly revenue jumped 1,127% on a year-over-year basis in the third quarter. Last month, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI closed the quarter with $50 billion in net annualized revenue, which represented a 77% year-over-year increase. The company’s growth was driven by its enterprise business, which saw sales more than double. The latest addition to OpenAI’s enterprise portfolio debuted on Thursday. GPT-6 Cyber can perform most cybersecurity tasks better than GPT-6 Astra, the company’s most capable general-purpose model. OpenAI engineers used it to develop 948 Linux⁠ exploits and uncover 81 high-severity zero-day flaws in Firefox. OpenAI President Greg Brockman revealed on Wednesday that the company had experienced a slowdown in the first half of the year. Its growth started accelerating after the June launch of GPT-5.6 Sol, the immediate predecessor to GPT-6 Astra. Brockman added that OpenAI’s ChatGPT Work productivity application and coding tools played a role as well. The company plans to go public sometime in 2027. Today’s cash infusion should make it easier for OpenAI to finance its steep infrastructure expenses until the listing. In July, The Information reported that the ChatGPT developer has more than $665 billion worth of chip and data center commitments. OpenAI has developed a custom inference accelerator in collaboration with Broadcom Inc. as part of an effort to lower its long-term hardware spending. Anthropic, for its part, is expected to kick off its IPO roadmap next week. The company reportedly plans to go public before Thanksgiving. sources.name: Canaltech
sources.title: Como usar o mapa do Gemini para encontrar novos lugares?
sources.text: Por Viviane França • Editado por Jones Oliveira | 07/11/2026 às 14:00 O Google lançou uma nova ferramenta chamada “Mapa” para o aplicativo Gemini em celulares. Com ela, você pode escolher uma região no mapa e pedir à inteligência artificial informações, recomendações e sugestões relacionadas ao local selecionado. A ferramenta é útil para quem quer encontrar restaurantes, pontos turísticos, lojas ou outros lugares de interesse sem precisar informar apenas o nome de uma cidade ou bairro. Ao abrir o recurso, o Gemini mostra um mapa da região atual do celular com uma área circular destacada . Você pode arrastar o mapa, aproximar ou afastar a visualização para posicionar a área sobre o local que deseja pesquisar. Também dá para procurar outro endereço ou região pelo ícone de lupa no canto superior direito. Depois de encontrar o local desejado, toque em “Explorar esta área”. O Gemini adiciona automaticamente a etiqueta “Área do Mapa” à caixa de texto, indicando que a região selecionada fará parte do contexto da conversa. A partir daí, é só fazer a pergunta ou enviar uma instrução, como pedir restaurantes próximos, pontos turísticos ou lugares interessantes para visitar. O recurso “Mapa” já está disponível nos aplicativos Gemini para Android e iOS , mas ainda não chegou à versão web. A ferramenta aparece no menu aberto pelo botão “+”, ao lado de opções Fotos, Câmera, Avatar, Arquivos, Drive e Notebooks. Caso você não queira adicionar uma região à conversa, basta tocar no botão “X” para fechar o mapa. Confira o passo a passo para começar a usar o mapa no Gemini: Deslize o carrossel de opções até encontrar “Mapa”; Permita que o Gemini acesse sua localização; Arraste o mapa e ajuste o zoom até encontrar a região desejada; Faça perguntas sobre o local ou peça sugestões de lugares para o Gemini. Se você gostou do conteúdo, talvez também se interesse por conferir “ 16 comandos para usar o Gemini no Google Maps ”.

sources.title: Cómo usar Gemini para encontrar, analizar y comparar productos antes de comprarlos
sources.text: Aplicaciones como ChatGPT, Claude o Gemini se han convertido en imprescindibles para millones de personas que buscan responder sus preguntas , obtener una explicación sobre algo que no entienden o, simplemente, obtener mejores resultados al buscar por internet . Y si hablamos de búsquedas online, muchas de ellas tienen que ver con comprar un producto o contratar un servicio . De ahí que existan tantos comparadores de viajes, telefonía, compañías eléctricas, electrónica o videojuegos. Es más. Comprar con Gemini o ChatGPT cada vez está más cerca de convertirse en una experiencia todo en uno. Este año hemos visto cómo Google ha ido incorporando elementos relacionados con las compras en sus productos y servicios . Como el carrito universal , que todavía no está presente en todos los países o las constantes mejoras del modo IA de Google y de Gemini enfocadas, precisamente a comprar por internet directamente desde su asistente de inteligencia artificial. Además, ya hemos visto con anterioridad que combinando Gemini y la cámara de tu móvil puedes organizar mejor tus compras . En este artículo vamos a ver de qué manera es posible comprar con Gemini . O, mejor dicho, qué cosas puedes pedirle a la IA de Google para ayudarte durante todo el proceso previo a la compra en sí. Por ejemplo, comparar precios, modelos del mismo producto, encontrar aquello que necesitas, inspirarte si no sabes qué regalar… En definitiva, Gemini puede ser un buen aliado y un asistente de compras si sabes cómo usarlo en tu favor. Comprar con Gemini puede resultar muy cómodo si sabes explicarle bien lo que necesitas . Primero, ¿sabes ya qué vas a comprar? Entonces, pídele que busque la tienda más barata. Si no estás seguro, pregúntale qué producto es mejor entre dos o tres que tengas en mente. Y si no tienes idea de lo que necesitas exactamente, expon tus necesidades y Gemini te dará las soluciones más aproximadas. Aquí van varios ejemplos de prompts sobre compras para empezar: En resumen, al buscar algo en Gemini, deberías tener en cuenta : Gemini nos da una plantilla para hacer una búsqueda de este tipo: “Quiero comprar [producto] para [uso concreto]. Presupuesto: [cantidad]. Debe cumplir: [requisitos imprescindibles]. Prefiero evitar: [restricciones]. Busca opciones disponibles en España, compáralas en una tabla con precio, especificaciones, ventajas, inconvenientes, garantía y reseñas. Después, dame X finalistas, señala riesgos y dime qué comprobaría yo mismo antes de pagar.” Hay muchos parámetros que te hacen decidirte por un producto. Según lo que sea, tal vez te interese lo económico . En otros casos, buscarás que dure mucho y se rompa poco . Otros productos te interesarán más por si tiene piezas de sustitución o recargables baratos . Y, muchas veces, tal vez quieras conocer qué te conviene más si hay que elegir entre que sea bueno, bonito o barato. Así que procura decírselo cuando busques qué comprar con Gemini. Por ejemplo, si vas a comprar algo tan genérico como un teléfono móvil y no tienes un candidato concreto, puedes preguntarle a Gemini que te muestra las mejores opciones según diferentes parámetros : los de mejor calidad, los más económicos, los que mejor combinen calidad-precio… Así, la IA te los mostrará en grupos comparando todas las opciones y te será más fácil decidirte por uno u otro. Las tablas son un elemento visual muy práctico cuando no te decides por un modelo concreto de ese producto que quieres comprar. Si tienes cuatro o cinco opciones a elegir, una tabla te resolverá las dudas. Así que díselo a Gemini, indicando que incluya parámetros como precio final, características más destacadas, dimensiones, peso, garantía… Según qué estés buscando comprar, puedes pedir mil y una cosas que te decantarán por una u otra opción. Materiales de fabricación, opinión de los usuarios y de los expertos, si cumple con los estándares o normativas… No des por sentado que Gemini te va a proporcionar toda la información que necesitas. Especifícalo tú mismo para que la tabla resultante sea lo más completa posible. Cuanto más caro es lo que quieres comprar, más tiempo le dedicarás a la búsqueda . Con Gemini ocurre igual. Si se trata de comprar con Gemini algo que te supondrá un desembolso considerable de dinero, te conviene utilizar la función Deep Research . En castellano, investigación profunda. Le llevará más tiempo a la IA darte una respuesta. Pero esa respuesta será un informe más preciso sobre lo que estás buscando. Y merece la pena. Además, en el modo Deep Research de Gemini puedes incluir tus propias fuentes . Por ejemplo, buscando tus propias fuentes en Google o subiendo archivos de manuales, prospectos, catálogos o folletos de productos. Así te asegurarás de que la IA busque donde tú quieres y te dé la información acorde a fuentes que tú consideres fiables o de confianza. Dedícale tiempo a esto antes de lanzar tu pregunta a Gemini y obtendrás mejores respuestas . Otra manera de ayudarte a decidirte entre dos o tres productos similares consiste en ver qué dicen los demás. Aunque las reseñas y opiniones tienen sus más y sus menos, y a veces hay que cogerlas con pinzas, pueden servir de ayuda. Así que pídele a Gemini que te diga qué opiniones merecen en internet determinado producto y si hay quejas o polémicas . Esto sirve tanto para el producto o servicio como para la tienda o proveedor del servicio . Hay tiendas y comercios en los que confiamos a ciegas. Pero es posible que encuentres un nuevo sitio con buenos precios que quieras probar. Si no lo conoces, necesitarás opiniones favorables que te hagan confiar en él. O, al contrario, que te libren de una mala experiencia. Pregunta si la compra es segura , si el envío es correcto, si hay atención al cliente , sede física, si el servicio posterior a la compra es el adecuado… Toda precaución es poca cuando se trata de comprar. sources.title: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
sources.text: Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips. Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips. China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times . The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says. Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new. The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang , was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

sources.title: Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS
sources.text: Conversational AI is transforming how humans interact with technology. From virtual assistants and AI-powered contact centers to real-time translation and accessibility tools, voice-first interfaces are rapidly becoming the default mode of interaction for millions of users worldwide. Yet delivering a truly natural voice experience remains one of the hardest challenges in AI infrastructure. Users expect human-like responsiveness. Excess latency can break conversational flow and erode trust. To feel natural, AI-generated speech must arrive within the same temporal window as human turn-taking. This post introduces how Cartesia , an AWS Partner specializing in real-time voice AI, uses purpose-built State Space Models (SSMs) and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale. Developers can build voice experiences that feel indistinguishable from human conversation. The demand for real-time voice AI is growing rapidly across industries: Traditional transformer-based text-to-speech (TTS) models struggle with streaming latency because they process entire sequences before producing output. This architectural limitation creates a fundamental tension: higher quality often means higher latency. A new class of models, State Space Models, resolves this trade-off. State Space Models (SSMs) take a fundamentally different approach to processing sequences than transformers, the architecture behind most of today’s AI. Transformers use a mechanism called attention, which compares every element in a sequence to every other element. As a result, the amount of computation grows quadratically as the sequence gets longer. SSMs instead treat a sequence as a system that evolves continuously over time, processing it step by step and carrying a compact internal state forward. This can be converted into a form computers handle efficiently, keeping the cost low for certain long sequences. This efficiency makes SSMs well suited to real-time, streaming data like live speech. Key advantages of SSMs for audio processing include: These properties make SSMs uniquely suited for real-time voice applications where both quality and latency are non-negotiable. Cartesia puts these SSM advantages to work in two production voice models: Sonic for speech generation and Ink for transcription. Cartesia is a real-time multimodal intelligence company that has built a voice AI application, purpose-built on State Space Model architecture. Founded by researchers who pioneered SSM advances, Cartesia’s application is designed for streaming inference at the edge of human perception. The application features two core models, Sonic for text-to-speech and Ink for speech-to-text, both optimized for sub-100ms first-byte latency while maintaining studio-quality output. Sonic is Cartesia’s flagship streaming text-to-speech model, delivering ultra-realistic speech synthesis with sub-100ms latency: Sonic is recommended for teams that want the fastest time-to-production with minimal operational overhead. Call the API and receive streaming audio in real time. Ink is Cartesia’s streaming speech-to-text model, purpose-built for conversational AI applications: Together, Sonic and Ink provide the complete voice AI stack needed to build conversational agents that feel human. If you need data sovereignty, latency control, or compliance, you can deploy Cartesia models directly into your own AWS account. Sonic is delivered as an Amazon SageMaker AI model package through AWS Marketplace, which you deploy to a SageMaker AI endpoint running entirely within your virtual private cloud (VPC). Inference data doesn’t leave your account. The deployment patterns in this section cover Sonic. Ink is currently available through the Cartesia API, which you can purchase through the Cartesia Voice AI Platform listing in AWS Marketplace. Two primary patterns are available for Sonic. Deploying on Amazon SageMaker AI is the fastest path to a managed, in-VPC Sonic endpoint. Sonic ships as an AWS Marketplace model package, so there’s a one-time subscribe step that grants your account an AWS Region-specific model-package ARN. You then create the SageMaker AI endpoint from that ARN, either from the console or with the SageMaker or Boto3 SDK. The following steps follow Cartesia’s official deployment notebook. Run from an Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instance or SageMaker Studio. The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role needs AmazonSageMakerFullAccess . To subscribe, your role (and you) need aws-marketplace:Subscribe , aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe , and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions . Otherwise, the account must already be subscribed to the listing. Before deployment, choose a supported instance type from the model package’s SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes field: If your chosen instance type’s applied value is below your current usage plus your planned endpoint instance count, you may need to request a service quota increase. See SageMaker AI quotas for details. In Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, you can subscribe to its AWS Marketplace model package, create a SageMaker model, and host it on a real-time endpoint. The following four steps show the deployment path. stories.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
stories.summary: Learn how to build a governed semantic layer for agentic AI inside EDB Postgres AI and query it from a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Business meaning, join paths, and access control all live in Postgres, with GRANT and row-level security enforcing what each agent can read.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: In this post, we show how to build a semantic layer for agentic AI using EDB Postgres AI . We run a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that queries the layer to answer customer 360 (C360) questions. Earlier posts in this series built the same C360 pattern with Stardog’s knowledge graph , Denodo’s data virtualization platform , AtScale’s dimensional model , and Strategy Mosaic’s linked models . EDB Postgres AI puts the semantic layer inside the operational Postgres database as an AIDB extension . Business meaning lives next to the data in standard Postgres COMMENT statements, the join graph comes from Postgres foreign keys, and governance uses Postgres GRANT and row-level security through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that ships with AIDB. An agent that answers business questions from live data needs three layers: a model that plans and writes queries, a meaning layer that tells the agent what the data represents, and a runtime that hosts the agent and controls identity and access. The Stardog post in this series introduced this framing. The model layer in this post is Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock , the same as prior posts (model availability varies by AWS Region ). The runtime layer is AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore Gateway handles inbound authorization, and AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, holds outbound credentials for the tool targets, same as prior posts. EDB Postgres AI hosts agents and tools inside the database itself and acts as the connection point for external agents through its MCP endpoint. The meaning layer is where this post diverges from the others. Here it is a SemKB that lives inside the operational Postgres database. The schema and the business definitions are indexed together. Postgres GRANT , row-level security, and column-level grants enforce access, not an advisory system prompt. The sections that follow cover how AIDB builds the layer, how AgentCore exposes it, and how two Postgres roles asking the same question get different answers. The dataset is the Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit , loaded into a single EDB Postgres AI instance in a dedicated c360 schema. The data model has four tables and one derived view. The physical schema is a plain Postgres join graph: a customer in the customers table lives at a location , places purchases , and each purchase references a product. The semantic work rests on three business ideas that column names don’t reveal. State isn’t on the customer row. It lives in locations , reached through the customers.location foreign key, and a comment on that column tells SemKB where to find it. purchases.price records the order total. An agent that reads it as a unit price and multiplies by quantity returns $502,529 for the top customer instead of $27,991.66. Big spender is a term the business owns. Captured as a view with a COMMENT ON VIEW statement, its definition stays in one place that every agent, dashboard, and query reads from. The questions we run through the agent end to end: The following diagram shows the request path from the analyst through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to the semantic layer inside EDB Postgres AI. The analyst authenticates with Amazon Cognito and calls AgentCore Gateway with the issued JSON Web Token (JWT) as a Bearer token. Gateway routes to AgentCore runtime, which plans with Claude on Amazon Bedrock. The agent calls MCP tools through Gateway, which forwards to an Application Load Balancer in the EDB Postgres AI virtual private cloud (VPC) and on to the edb-endpoints MCP server inside AIDB. AIDB serves the SemKB, semantic aliases, and read-only PostgreSQL tables. AgentCore traces go to Amazon CloudWatch, and AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces as rows in the aidb_otel schema inside Postgres. Figure 1: Reference architecture for EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Two flows cross the boundary between AgentCore and EDB Postgres AI. Inbound: A client calls AgentCore Gateway with a bearer token issued by an Amazon Cognito user pool . The Gateway inbound JWT authorizer validates the token against the Cognito discovery URL. Gateway then evaluates its Cedar policy against the token’s claims to decide which tools this agent, acting for this user, can invoke. It then routes the call to AgentCore runtime. The agent invokes Claude on Amazon Bedrock for planning and answer composition. Outbound to the semantic layer: The agent’s tool call is an MCP request. AgentCore Gateway supports MCP server targets directly. AIDB’s edb-endpoints HTTP server speaks streamable HTTP MCP with HTTP Basic authentication , which lets Gateway treat it as an MCP server target with no translation layer. An Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate fronts edb-endpoints on an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance. The ALB URL is registered as the Gateway target. The AgentCore Identity credential provider holds the Postgres role credential and injects it as Basic auth on every outbound request. The agent code doesn’t see the Postgres credential. Observability: AgentCore emits traces for tool calls, large language model (LLM) calls, and token usage to CloudWatch Transaction Search . AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema inside Postgres, queryable with ordinary SQL after the database is configured to write them (see enabling telemetry on the source database ). No AWS Lambda is required in this architecture. AIDB already speaks MCP, so Gateway talks to it as an MCP server target directly through the ALB. The Denodo post in this series uses the same ALB pattern in front of its MCP server, and the architecture here is unchanged other than the vendor. These steps assume AIDB is installed and enabled on the EDB Postgres AI instance and the Stardog C360 kit’s four CSVs are loaded into a dedicated c360 schema with the primary and foreign keys

stories.title: How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search
stories.summary: Gen Digital built Norton Revamp, a generative AI-powered professional reputation management platform, with an AI-curated News Engine grounded by Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. See how the Gen team delivers real-time, cited content suggestions, goal setting, and news feeds with zero data egress and Norton-grade privacy.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search
sources.text: Your professional reputation now lives online first. Recruiters check LinkedIn before returning a call. Clients review your digital presence before booking a first meeting. For ambitious professionals, that shift is an opportunity: a well-crafted online voice can open doors that a résumé alone never could. But standing out takes more than content generation. It takes real-time awareness of what’s happening right now. A professional building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader needs to react to today’s breakthroughs, not last week’s headlines. And with feeds flooded by AI-generated noise, audiences reward authenticity and timeliness more than ever. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore made that possible. We built Norton Revamp , a generative AI-powered professional reputation management platform. At its heart is an AI-curated News Engine, powered by AgentCore Web Search, that grounds every content suggestion, goal recommendation, and news feed item in current, cited web knowledge. The platform launched in March 2026, built by a small group of engineers. In this post, we show you how the Gen team builds an AI-curated News Engine in Norton Revamp with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search to help customers turn ideas into engaging social media posts. Unlike chatbots that rely on static knowledge bases, Norton Revamp needs to understand what’s trending right now in each user’s professional domain. A cyber security expert needs today’s threat intelligence. A marketing leader needs this week’s industry shifts. Traditional approaches (custom web crawlers, third-party news APIs, static content databases) each carry trade-offs: infrastructure overhead, stale data, vendor complexity, or data egress risk. We evaluated three alternatives before choosing AgentCore Web Search. Custom crawlers require ongoing maintenance and lag real time. Third-party news APIs added vendor contracts, API key management, and data leaving our AWS environment. Static knowledge bases were perpetually stale. AgentCore Web Search eliminated these concerns. It’s fully managed with zero infrastructure overhead, operates entirely within AWS with zero data egress, and returns cited sources with URLs and publication dates. This makes personalized, real-time news feeds viable at scale. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a fully managed web search capability, compliant with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It’s available as a managed connector on the AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Our agent sends a natural-language query, and Web Search returns relevant snippets, source URLs, titles, and publication dates that the model uses to produce grounded responses. This capability powers three core features: Every user gets a personalized content stream surfacing the latest articles and trending topics tied to their goal. If you’re building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader, your feed prioritizes AI breakthroughs, industry analysis, and emerging use cases, sourced in real time through AgentCore Web Search. Unlike a static RSS aggregator, the feed is a goal-aware discovery engine that refreshes with every session. Users receive AI-generated content ideas tailored to trending topics in their space, written in their own authentic voice, with optional AI-generated visuals. AgentCore Web Search grounds every suggestion on what’s happening today . A three-step coaching flow (Analyze, Refine, Post) walks users from initial ideas to published content on LinkedIn and X, with a feedback loop, so the AI gets sharper with every iteration. Users define a goal. The AI builds a personalized roadmap with weekly themes and milestones. AgentCore Web Search feeds real-time trend data into goal generation, so weekly themes reflect current industry movements. The system learns from the past four weeks of activity, refreshing recommendations as users grow. Figure 1: Event-driven architecture of the Norton Revamp News Engine The integration follows an event-driven architecture. When a user sets or updates their professional goal, Amazon Nova (through Amazon Bedrock) generates targeted search queries based on the goal, recent activity, and engagement patterns. The agent sends these queries to AgentCore Web Search, which returns cited results entirely within our AWS environment. Our AI Learning System ranks the results for relevance, recency, and source credibility. The ranked results then serve as grounding context for Amazon Nova Lite to generate content suggestions in the user’s authentic voice. Engagement data feeds back into query generation, making the News Engine progressively smarter. Generative AI and machine learning stack: Infrastructure: React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS on the frontend. Node.js, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB (multi-table with composite key patterns), Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon EventBridge, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS Secrets Manager on the backend. Infrastructure managed through Terraform with blue-green deployment for zero-downtime releases. Processing pipeline: The platform runs four pipeline stages: We embedded generative AI from day one, as both the product and the development methodology. The human-AI responsibility split was deliberate: human-owned architecture decisions, security reviews, business logic, and personalization algorithms. AI handled code generation, documentation, test scaffolding, refactoring, and UI component creation. With Claude, we produced 10 or more design variants per concept, compressed design-to-prototype time from weeks to hours and generated 70 percent of UI code with AI. We tested five pricing models in the time previously needed for one. The gamification system went through eight iterations before launching. The measurable impact: 3x faster feature implementation, boilerplate generation accele

sources.title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity. When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer. Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories. In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it. U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud. Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration. The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars. AiDaH started with a principle: think big, start small. U Mobile began conceptualization in late 2025 with two pilot agents and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability. A Q1 2026 pilot brought the internal IT helpdesk online with 4 agents and 20 operational scenarios. Through 2026 the platform hardened and expanded, adding three-tier routing and reaching 6 agents by mid-year. AiDaH went live to 50 L2 call center and branch users in Q3 2026 with 8 agents, and now covers more than 150 documented operational scenarios. The difference between traditional AI assistance and agentic AI is best illustrated through a real example. With a traditional AI assistant, a support agent handling “mobile data not working overseas” gets help drafting a response and some suggested troubleshooting steps, but still manually checks roaming status, verifies eligibility, raises tickets, and sends the final reply. With AiDaH, the system independently checks the subscriber’s roaming configuration, verifies international data eligibility, and identifies the specific point of failure. It then assembles a remediation plan: which services to reset, what configuration to push, and whether a network ticket is warranted. The support agent reviews and confirms, and the actions execute. The investigation that used to consume the agent’s time now happens before they read the first line. The human decision point is preserved where it matters: at the moment something changes on a live subscriber account. In one production case, a subscriber reported being unable to purchase an add-on. AiDaH traced the failure to an error code, “Subscriber has pending order.” It also revealed that the customer had attempted the same purchase more than 30 times across multiple channels over three days, every attempt blocked by the same underlying pending order. AiDaH surfaced the root cause and the remediation steps in a single response. Previously that would have required manual investigation across several systems. AiDaH runs on a layered architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, deployed in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region. Staff interact through Microsoft Teams, a deliberate choice to meet most users where they already work, with no new application to learn and no portal switching. The following diagram shows how the layers fit together. As shown in Figure 1, the platform is organized into six layers. Staff reach AiDaH through Microsoft Teams and a web portal served by Amazon CloudFront and protected by AWS WAF, with an AWS Lambda backend and a REST API for programmatic triggers. The routing brain on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Every request passes a pre-flight security check covering role-based access control, identity validation, and guardrails,

sources.title: How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: Greenlight Financial resolves more than 90 percent of up to 4,000 security and risk cases each month without human intervention. Greenlight’s Luna uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , infrastructure for building, connecting, and optimizing agents at scale. Specifically, Greenlight uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to host Luna’s agent code. It uses AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to support its tiered multi-agent system. This avoids the need to build and operate these capabilities in-house. Luna triages dark web breach-card alerts, identity anomalies, and financial-risk events in seconds. This post explains how Greenlight Financial built an autonomous security operations center (SOC) solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover its multi-tiered supervisor architecture, more than 30 specialized agents, episodic memory for continuous learning, and expansion from SOC use cases into financial risk triage. We share production metrics, infrastructure decisions, and patterns for building autonomous security operations in regulated industries. Greenlight Financial provides financial products for families: debit cards, savings tools, and connected devices such as the Family Hub and Pet Tracker. The company processes sensitive financial data at scale under the same regulatory requirements as major banks. Greenlight’s SOC receives 3,000–4,000 security and risk alerts per month from four primary vectors: Each alert demands cross-referencing multiple data sources before an analyst can render a verdict. A single dark web breach card notification requires checking whether the card is active, deduplicating against prior notifications, reviewing customer session data, and checking open support tickets. This workflow takes a human analyst 15-30 minutes per case. At 4,000 cases per month, that math breaks. Greenlight built Luna as a hierarchical multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture follows a tiered supervisor pattern that mirrors how human SOC teams operate. L1 handles volume, and L2 handles complexity. Figure 1: Luna’s tiered supervisor architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Tier 1 supervisor uses an advanced language model available through Amazon Bedrock running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime within an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). The runtime uses private subnets and direct code deployment through a ZIP file and Amazon Simple Storage Service ( Amazon S3 ). It handles initial triage of incoming cases by orchestrating more than 30 specialized agents: The Tier 1 supervisor receives cases through two paths: Amazon API Gateway, which exposes the Luna Queue API and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint, and Tines SOAR for automated alert ingestion. It determines which specialized agents to invoke based on alert type, synthesizes their findings, and renders a verdict. The median triage time for routine cases is single-digit seconds. Cases that exceed Tier 1’s confidence threshold escalate to a Tier 2 supervisor using an advanced foundation model on Amazon Bedrock with extended reasoning capabilities. This agent handles the 10 percent of cases that require multi-step reasoning: The Tier 2 supervisor runs on a scheduled basis, using Amazon EventBridge rate triggers and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) queue completions to batch-process escalated cases, and on demand for urgent Tier 1-escalated cases. Different teams engage Luna in different ways, so the application exposes three entry points. These range from fully automated alert ingestion to interactive, on-demand investigation. Each entry point maps to a persona and how their work arrives: The memory layer is built on AgentCore memory. This layer is what separates Luna from a stateless triage tool. It supports pattern recognition, deduplication, and continuous accuracy improvement. Stores recent events and resolution outcomes. When a new alert arrives, Luna checks: “Have I seen this pattern in the last 30 days? What was the verdict? Is this a known behavior that I should allowlist?” Concrete example: A Greenlight infrastructure role generates a specific access pattern every Tuesday at 3 AM for scheduled maintenance. Without memory, Luna would flag this every week. With episodic memory, Luna learned after the first resolution that this pattern is expected and auto-allowlists it. Persists semantic preferences and resolution templates beyond the 30-day window: A dedicated pipeline feeds resolution outcomes back into the system: This pipeline drove Luna’s autonomous resolution rate from 83 percent (Tier 1 only) to more than 90 percent (Tier 1, Tier 2, and learnings). Greenlight expanded Luna into financial risk assessment within two months of the SOC deployment. The architectural changes were minimal: new specialized agents and a risk-domain supervisor layered onto the existing infrastructure. When a Greenlight customer card appears on the dark web, Luna executes this workflow autonomously: Greenlight receives hundreds of breach card notifications daily. Luna processes each in seconds. A human analyst doing the same work, logging into Galileo, checking DynamoDB, opening Mixpanel, searching Zendesk, takes 15-30 minutes per card. The following table tracks Greenlight’s security operations on the metrics that matter most to the SOC. It compares three stages: manual triage before Luna, Tier 1 automation, and the full Tier 1 and Tier 2 system. Based on Greenlight’s case volume and manual handling-time measurements, processing 4,000 cases at 15–30 minutes each would require approximately 1,000–2,000 analyst hours per month. Greenlight reports that Luna autonomously resolves more than 90 percent of these cases, avoiding an estimated 900–1,800 hours of routine manual work each month. stories.title: ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
stories.summary: Learn how to configure Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway for an on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID, so an AI agent can call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the calling user's identity. AgentCore Gateway performs the exchange natively, with no interceptor Lambda or custom code.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
sources.text: AI agents that interact with enterprise APIs on behalf of users need to maintain user identity throughout the request chain. Without identity propagation, API calls arrive at downstream services as the application itself rather than the user who initiated the action. This breaks audit trails, bypasses user-level access controls, and violates the principle of least privilege. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post shows how to configure AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for an on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID. An AI agent can then call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the calling user’s identity. You configure the token exchange on the gateway target, and AgentCore Gateway performs the exchange on each request. The pattern can be applied to other REST APIs protected by OAuth. In production, you can additionally pair identity propagation with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful content and validate the agent’s inputs and outputs. The architecture involves three key components connected through AgentCore Gateway: The following figure shows the end-to-end solution architecture, including components within AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow. Figure 1: Solution architecture across AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow As shown in Figure 1, the user acquires a JSON Web Token (JWT) to invoke the agent 1. The agent authenticates to the gateway with a JWT token scoped to the agent’s own application registration 2. The gateway then exchanges that token, using the OBO flow, for a new token scoped to the ServiceNow API connector, with the original user’s identity preserved 3. ServiceNow receives a valid token whose preferred_username claim maps to an existing ServiceNow user and applies that user’s permissions to the API call 4. When the agent calls the gateway, it presents a JWT with an audience claim matching the agent’s client ID (for example, 3ff88e17-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX ). ServiceNow, however, expects a token with an audience claim matching its own API connector client ID ( 5d4a7a11-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX ). The OBO flow bridges this gap. AgentCore Gateway sends the inbound token to the Entra token endpoint along with the agent application’s client credentials, the target scope, and a parameter requested_token_use: on_behalf_of . Entra validates that the calling user consented to the delegation, then issues a new token for the ServiceNow API with the original user’s claims intact. Before you begin, you need the following: Start by creating an application registration to represent the ServiceNow API connector. The following screenshot shows the application registration page for the ServiceNow API Connector in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 2: Application registration for the ServiceNow API connector in Microsoft Entra ID After creating, in the Overview page note the Application (client) ID. In the navigation menu expand Manage and select Expose an API and add a scope named user_impersonation using the default Application ID URI. This scope is what the OBO flow requests when exchanging tokens. The following screenshot shows how to expose an API in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 3: Exposing the user_impersonation scope in Microsoft Entra ID Next, create an application registration for the AI agent. The following screenshot shows the application registration page in Microsoft Entra ID for the ServiceNow Agent application. Figure 4: Application registration for the ServiceNow Agent in Microsoft Entra ID Note the Application (client) ID for the ServiceNowAgent. Create a client secret on this registration. The gateway needs these credentials to perform the OBO exchange. The following screenshot shows how you can create a client secret on the ServiceNow Agent application registration in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 5: Creating a client secret on the ServiceNow Agent application registration Then configure the agent application to have API permissions to call the ServiceNow API connector application. The following screenshot shows the API permissions that you need to configure on the ServiceNow Agent application registration in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 6: API permission configuration in Microsoft Entra ID No changes to the Entra configuration are needed beyond what you would set up for any standard OBO integration between two applications. In the ServiceNow administrative console, navigate to System OAuth > Inbound Integrations and create a new inbound integration (Third party ID token issued by OIDC supporting identity provider). Specify the client ID from the ServiceNow API connector application registration you created in Entra. The following screenshot shows the configuration of the inbound integration in ServiceNow. Figure 7: Configuring the inbound integration in ServiceNow In the same screen, create a new OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider configuration and enter the OIDC metadata URL for your Entra tenant. Map the user claim to the appropriate user field. For example, if your Entra tenant places the user’s email in the preferred_username claim, map that to the Email field in ServiceNow. Clear JTI verification if your Entra tenant doesn’t include it in tokens. Entra uses an internal claim named uti on tokens it issues, which is equivalent to JTI. Consider mapping this uti claim to a jti claim to provide additional replay protection and denylisting. The following screenshot shows how to configure the OIDC provider in ServiceNow. Figure 8: Configuring the OAuth OIDC provider in ServiceNow Finally, in the same screen, create an auth scope for the integration (for example, APIConnector ). The following screenshot shows how to create a new auth scope in ServiceNow. Figure 9: Creating a new auth scope in ServiceNow Limit the auth scope to the Table API, or whichever ServiceNow APIs your agent needs to access, as shown in the following screen

stories.title: Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick
stories.summary: Amazon Quick brings structured and unstructured data together in one experience. In this post, you connect Amazon S3 as a knowledge base, enrich a dataset, build a Space, and create a custom chat agent that answers business questions across both data types through a single conversational interface.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick
sources.text: Organizations collect data in many forms. Structured data lives in databases and spreadsheets, whereas unstructured data sits in documents, reports, and files stored across file systems. Analyzing both together typically requires switching between multiple tools, running separate queries, and manually correlating results. Amazon Quick addresses this with a unified experience. You can connect structured data through enriched datasets and unstructured data through S3-backed knowledge bases . You can then query both through a single conversational AI agent. The following diagram illustrates how each component connects to deliver a unified data experience through Amazon Quick. Figure 1: Solution architecture for combining structured and unstructured data in Amazon Quick With this layered approach, you can expand the solution over time. When you add a new data source to the Space, the agent linked to that Space can use it, and responses respect the permissions of the user who asks. To follow along with this walkthrough, you need: Unstructured documents: Upload these to your Amazon S3 bucket for the knowledge base: Structured data: Download this file to your computer. You upload it directly to Amazon Quick in Step 3: Start by connecting Amazon Quick to your S3 bucket. From the Amazon Quick console, select Knowledge in the left navigation panel. The knowledge page shows available connector types, including Amazon Q Business, Web Crawler, Amazon S3, and third-party options like Google Drive, OneDrive, and Microsoft SharePoint. Under Amazon S3, choose Add . In the Create S3 knowledge base dialog, on the Connect S3 bucket page, provide the following details: Figure 2: Create integration dialog showing the S3 connection fields After the S3 integration is created, Amazon Quick prompts you to create a knowledge base. The knowledge base indexes your S3 content for AI-powered search. Next: Additional settings opens optional settings for document-level access control lists (ACLs) and a metadata files folder. Decide whether to use ACLs before you create the knowledge base, because you can’t change that choice later. This walkthrough uses sample data, so the default settings are sufficient. For details, see Set up and manage Amazon S3 integration . Choose Create . A success banner confirms the S3 integration, and the knowledge base begins indexing in the background. Figure 3: Create knowledge base dialog with the Business Knowledge Base name and content options A dataset is your structured data file loaded into Amazon Quick. By enriching the dataset with semantic descriptions, custom instructions, and correct data types, the AI agent can interpret your data more accurately. It can then translate natural language questions into SQL queries. Amazon Quick ingests the file into SPICE (the in-memory calculation engine) and the dataset appears in your dataset list. The dataset takes its name from the uploaded file, so it appears as Product_Sales.csv in your account. Enriching your dataset with semantic information helps the AI understand your data in business context. The agent uses this context to translate natural language questions into more accurate SQL queries. From the dataset page, choose Edit dataset to enter the data preparation view. In the Transform tab, update data types for columns that were auto-detected incorrectly. For this dataset: Figure 4: Transform view showing data type changes applied to the Product_Sales.csv dataset Select the Output tab to access the dataset-level enrichment fields. Here you provide context that helps the AI understand what your data represents and how to use it. Description: Add a dataset-level description: “Product sales transaction data for AnyCompany, covering orders from FY2024-FY2025 across North America, EMEA, Asia Pacific, and Latin America. Includes order details, customer information, product lines, and revenue metrics.” Custom instructions: Add guidance for how the AI should query this data: TAGS: Sales, revenue, orders, regional performance, product analytics Column descriptions: Select each column in the left panel and add a description. For example: Figure 5: Output view showing dataset details with Description and Custom instructions configured Choose Save & publish to save your changes. The dataset summary now shows the columns with their correct data types and the descriptions you added. Figure 6: Enriched Product_Sales.csv dataset summary showing all 16 columns, data types, and descriptions This enriched dataset provides the structured data layer for your solution. When the agent receives a natural language question about sales data, it uses these descriptions and instructions to generate more accurate SQL queries. Combined with the knowledge base from Step 2, you now have both structured and unstructured data ready to bring together in a Space. Spaces in Amazon Quick act as unified data workspaces. A Space can hold file uploads, dashboards, knowledge bases, actions, and datasets, giving your chat agent a single location to query across data types. From the left navigation, select Spaces and create a new Space. Name it “Business Intelligence Hub”. Add your knowledge base and dataset to the Space: The Space now shows both your knowledge base (unstructured documents) and your enriched dataset (structured sales data) linked as data sources. This is the central hub where both data types come together, giving your chat agent a single place to query across everything. Figure 7 shows the Space with both resources in the Ready state. Figure 7: Business Intelligence Hub Space showing the Product_Sales.csv dataset and Business Knowledge Base Navigate to Chat agents in the left navigation and choose Create chat agent . Amazon Quick presents a prompt builder where you can describe your agent in natural language or choose from templates like Training Guide, Project Coordinator, and Onboarding Helper. For this walkthrough, choose Skip to configure the agent manually.
